Course Theme:
Abstraction Is Good, But Don't Forget Reality
Most CS and CE courses emphasize abstraction
Abstract data types
Asymptotic analysis
These abstractions have limits
Especially in the presence of bugs
Need to understand details of underlying implementations
Why it matters
An abstraction states what a component promises, not how it fails or how fast it runs.
When abstractions leak, only the implementation model explains the observed behavior.

Carnegie Mellon
Great Reality #1:
Ints Are Not Integers, Floats Are Not Reals
Example 1: Is x² ≥ 0?
Float's:  Yes!
Int's:
40000*40000 → 1600000000
50000*50000 → ??
2,500,000,000 > 2,147,483,647 (TMax)
w=32: the product overflows and wraps
Example 2: Is (x + y) + z = x + (y + z)?
Unsigned & Signed Int's:  Yes!
Float's:
(1e20 + -1e20) + 3.14 --> 3.14
1e20 + (-1e20 + 3.14) --> ??
-1e20 + 3.14 rounds back to -1e20
3.14 is below the precision of 1e20
Answer to Example 2 (why float addition is not associative)
(1e20 + -1e20) + 3.14  -->  3.14     # 1e20 + -1e20 = 0 exactly
 1e20 + (-1e20 + 3.14) -->  0.0      # -1e20 + 3.14 = -1e20 (rounds)
Cause: finite precision. Representable floats near 1e20 are spaced far apart, so adding
3.14 cannot change the value; the middle sum stays -1e20 and the outer sum is 0.0.
Integers: addition is exact and associative (ring). Floats: rounding breaks associativity.
Bryant and O'Hallaron, Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective, Third Edition
Source: CS:APP3e Ch. 2; Lecture 1, Slide 4

Carnegie Mellon
Computer Arithmetic
Does not generate random values
Arithmetic operations have important mathematical properties
Cannot assume all “usual” mathematical properties
Due to finiteness of representations
Integer operations
Satisfy “ring” properties:
•  Commutativity
•  Associativity
•  Distributivity
Limited range → overflow wraps
(modular arithmetic)
Floating-point operations
Satisfy “ordering” properties:
•  Monotonicity
•  Values of signs
Finite precision → rounding;
associativity fails (Slide 6)
Observation: need to understand which abstractions apply in which contexts —
important issues for compiler writers and serious application programmers.
Bryant and O'Hallaron, Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective, Third Edition
Source: Lecture 1, Slide 5
Textbook: CS:APP3e Ch. 2, Sec. 2.2-2.4 (Integer and Floating-Point Representation)

Section Summary:
Great Reality #1
Computer arithmetic is deterministic and structured,
not random: ints form a ring, floats obey ordering rules.
Finiteness breaks familiar algebra: 50000*50000 overflows;
(x+y)+z = x+(y+z) fails for floats (1e20 example).
x² ≥ 0: always true for floats, false for ints.
Implication: know which math abstractions hold when.

Great Reality #2:
You've Got to Know Assembly
The misconception
Chances are, you'll never write programs in assembly.
Compilers are much better & more patient than you are.
True for production code — but it does not make assembly knowledge useless.
The reality
Understanding assembly is key to the machine-level execution model:
•  Behavior of programs in presence of bugs — high-level language models break down
•  Tuning program performance — understand optimizations done / not done by the compiler
•  Understanding sources of program inefficiency
•  Implementing system software — compiler has machine code as target; OS manages process state
•  Creating / fighting malware — x86 assembly is the language of choice!
Bryant and O'Hallaron, Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective, Third Edition
Source: CS:APP3e Ch. 3; Lecture 1, Slide 6
Textbook: CS:APP3e Ch. 3, Sec. 3.1-3.2 (A Historical Perspective; Program Encodings)

Carnegie Mellon
Knowing Assembly: Critical Use Cases
Debugging & performance
•  Inspect machine-level state when the
high-level model breaks (bugs)
•  Verify which optimizations the compiler
did and did not apply
•  Locate sources of inefficiency at the
instruction level
System software & malware
•  Compilers take machine code as their
target
•  Operating systems must manage
process state
•  Creating / fighting malware: x86
assembly is the language of choice
Why the compiler argument does not settle it
Compilers act on your code as written. Assembly shows you the result of their decisions, so you
can shape source code that they compile well.
When a program misbehaves, no source-level model describes what happens — the machine-level
execution model is the only reliable description.
Bomblab (L2) and Attacklab (L3) exercise exactly this skill on x86-64 binaries.
Bryant and O'Hallaron, Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective, Third Edition

Section Summary:
Great Reality #2
You will rarely write assembly; compilers outperform you.
But assembly is the key to the machine-level execution model.
It explains behavior under bugs, where high-level models break.
It exposes compiler optimizations and sources of inefficiency.
It is required for system software (compilers, OS process state).
It is the weapon in creating and fighting malware (x86).

Great Reality #3:
Memory Matters — RAM Is an Unphysical Abstraction
Memory is not unbounded
It must be allocated and managed
Many applications are memory dominated
Memory referencing bugs are especially pernicious
Effects are distant in both time and space
Memory performance is not uniform
Cache and virtual memory effects can greatly affect program performance
Adapting program to characteristics of memory system can lead to major speed improvements

Byte map of struct_t

bytes 8-11  : d3 ... d0 (low half of d)
bytes 12-15 : d7 ... d4 (high half of d)

What each fun(i) writes
fun(0), fun(1): land in a[0], a[1]; d untouched → 3.14.
fun(2): clobbers low half of d (d3...d0) → 3.1399998664856.
fun(3): clobbers high half of d (d7...d4) → 2.00000061035156.
fun(4): hits padding bytes; d survives → 3.14 (this system).
fun(6): reaches beyond struct_t → segmentation fault.
Each write stores 1073741824 (= 2^30) into a[i].
An out-of-bounds write silently rewrites a logically unrelated variable (d).

Memory Referencing Errors
C and C++ do not provide any memory protection
Out of bounds array references
Invalid pointer values
Abuses of malloc/free
Can lead to nasty bugs
Whether or not bug has any effect depends on system and compiler
Action at a distance: corrupted object logically unrelated to the one being accessed
Effect of bug may be first observed long after it is generated
How can I deal with this?
•  Program in Java, Ruby, Python, ML, …  (they check references for you)
•  Understand what possible interactions may occur
•  Use or develop tools to detect referencing errors (e.g., Valgrind)
Bryant and O'Hallaron, Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective, Third Edition

Section Summary:
Great Reality #3
RAM as unbounded, uniform memory is an unphysical abstraction.
Memory must be allocated and managed; many apps are memory dominated.
C/C++ give no memory protection; out-of-bounds writes corrupt
unrelated objects — effects distant in time and space.
struct_t example: one bad store turns 3.14 into 2.00000061035156
or crashes the program (segmentation fault).
Cache/virtual-memory locality can change speed dramatically.

Great Reality #4:
There's More to Performance Than Asymptotic Complexity
Constant factors matter too!
And even exact op count does not predict performance
Easily see 10:1 performance range depending on how code is written
Must optimize at multiple levels: algorithm, data representations, procedures, and loops
Why op counts alone fail (reasons developed in this course)
•  Instructions differ in cost; one source line maps to many instructions
•  The memory hierarchy serves some accesses far faster than others (locality)
•  Access order (stride) decides whether data comes from cache or DRAM
•  So identical op counts can differ by large factors in real time
Must understand the system to optimize: how programs are compiled and executed,
how to measure performance and identify bottlenecks, and how to improve performance
without destroying code modularity and generality.
Bryant and O'Hallaron, Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective, Third Edition

Optimizing Performance: Multiple Levels
Must optimize at multiple levels
Algorithm — do less work
Data representations — layout that aids locality
Procedures and loops — trim per-iteration overhead
Must understand the system to optimize performance
How programs are compiled and executed
How to measure performance and identify bottlenecks
How to improve performance without destroying modularity and generality
Section summary (Great Reality #4)
Asymptotic complexity is necessary but not sufficient: constant factors and access patterns decide
real running time — 4.3 ms vs. 81.8 ms (19x) for identical copies; 10:1 ranges are common.

Great Reality #5:
Computers Do More Than Execute Programs
They need to get data in and out
•  I/O system is critical to program reliability and performance
•  Every result is useless if it cannot be read, written, or transmitted correctly
•  Course coverage: high-level and low-level I/O (Ch. 10)
They communicate with each other over networks
Many system-level issues arise in presence of network:
•  Concurrent operations by autonomous processes
•  Coping with unreliable media
•  Cross platform compatibility
•  Complex performance issues
Bryant and O'Hallaron, Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective, Third Edition

Great Reality #5
Computers also move data: I/O and networking are first-class.
The I/O system is critical to reliability and performance.
Networks add concurrency by autonomous processes,
unreliable media, cross-platform compatibility issues,
and complex performance questions.
Hence the final part of the course: I/O, networking,
concurrency — proxylab ties them together.

Course Perspective
Most systems courses are builder-centric
Computer Architecture — design a pipelined processor in Verilog
Operating Systems — implement sample portions of an operating system
Compilers — write a compiler for a simple language
Networking — implement and simulate network protocols
This course: user-centric
213 is unusual: instead of building a system, you learn how systems behave and how to
exploit that behavior as an application programmer.
You still build — bombs, caches, shells, allocators, proxies — but each lab teaches a system
behavior to exploit, not to construct.
That is why 213 serves as the foundation for all of the builder-centric courses.

Labs, Part 1: Programs, Data, and the Memory Hierarchy
L1 — Datalab
Manipulating bits. Two’s-complement and IEEE-754 bit puzzles.
Unit topics: bit operations, arithmetic; representation of C control and data structures; aspects of architecture and compilers.
L2 — Bomblab
Defusing a binary bomb: a program with secret phases, each needing one exact input string.
You disassemble x86-64 and read assembly — the machine-level execution model (Great Reality #2).
L3 — Attacklab
The basics of code injection attacks.
Exploits buffer overflow: writing past an array corrupts unrelated memory (Great Reality #3).
L4 — Cachelab
Building a cache simulator and optimizing for locality.
Learn how to exploit locality in your programs (memory mountain, copyij/copyji).
Bryant and O'Hallaron, Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective, Third Edition
Source: Lecture 1, Slides 30-31

Labs, Part 2: Control Flow, Virtual Memory, Networking
L5 — Tshlab
Writing your own Unix shell.
Unit topics: hardware exceptions, processes, process control, Unix signals, nonlocal jumps. A first introduction to
concurrency.
L6 — Malloclab
Writing your own malloc package.
Unit topics: virtual memory, address translation, dynamic storage allocation. Get a real feel for systems-level programming.
L7 — Proxylab
Writing your own Web proxy.
Unit topics: high- and low-level I/O, network programming, Internet services, Web servers, concurrency, concurrent server
design, threads, I/O multiplexing with select. Learn network programming and more about concurrency and synchronization.

Lab Rationale
Each lab has a well-defined goal
Such as solving a puzzle or winning a contest
Doing the lab should result in new skills and new concepts
We use competition in a fun and healthy way
Set a reasonable threshold for full credit
Post intermediate results (anonymized) on the Autolab scoreboard — for glory!
Why it works
A concrete goal makes the abstraction concrete: defeating the bomb is proof that you can read
assembly; beating the scoreboard proves your allocator or cache optimizer really is faster.
The threshold keeps credit attainable; the scoreboard motivates going beyond it.

Policies: Labs and Exams
Work groups: You must work alone on all lab assignments.
Handins: Labs due at 11:59pm on Tues or Thurs; electronic handins using Autolab (no exceptions!).
Exams: Online, in network-isolated clusters; held over multiple days; self-scheduled — just sign up!
Appealing grades: In writing to Prof O’Hallaron within 7 days of completion of grading; follow the formal
procedure in the syllabus.
Grading (Lecture 1, Slide 29)
•  Exams (50%): midterm (20%), final (30%)
•  Labs (50%): weighted according to effort
•  Final grades based on a straight scale
Also: laptops permitted; electronic communication forbidden; no recordings of ANY kind;
presence in lectures/recitations voluntary, recommended.

Timeliness
Grace days
5 grace days for the semester
Limit of 2 grace days per lab, used automatically
Covers scheduling crunch, out-of-town trips, illnesses,
minor setbacks
Save them until late in the term!
Lateness penalties
•  Once grace day(s) used up:
penalized 15% per day
•  No handins later than 3 days
after due date
Catastrophic events
•  Major illness, death in family, …
•  Formulate a plan (with your academic
advisor) to get back on track
Advice
Once you start running late, it's really hard to catch up.
Rationale: labs build on each other (bits → assembly → attacks → caches → shell → malloc → proxy),
so falling behind compounds across the sequence.

Cheating: Description and Consequences
What IS cheating
•  Sharing code: copying, retyping, looking at,
    or supplying a file
•  Describing: verbal description of code from
    one person to another
•  Coaching: helping your friend to write a lab,
    line by line
•  Searching the Web for solutions
•  Copying code from a previous course or
    online solution
Only code we supply, or from the CS:APP website, is allowed.
What is NOT cheating
•  Explaining how to use systems
or tools
•  Helping others with high-level
design issues
